source_text: Longum est ire per singula: nihil in homine membrorum est, quod non et necessitatis causa sit, et decoris: et quod magis mirum est, eadem figura omnibus, sed quaedam unicuique lineamenta deflexa. Sic et similes universi videmur, et inter se singulis dissimiles invenimur. Quid nascendi ratio? Quid cupido generandi? Nonne a Deo data est? et ut ubera partu maturescente lactescant, et ut tener foelus ubertate lactei roris adolescat? Nec universitati solummodo Deus, sed et partibus consulit. Britannia sole deficitur, sed circumfluentis maris tepore recreatur: Aegypti siccitatem temperat Nilus amnis: colit Euphrates Mesopotamiam: pro imbribus pensat Indus, et serere Orientem dicitur et rigare. Quod si ingressus aliquam domum, omnia exculta, disposita, ornata vidisses, utique praeesse ei crederes dominum, et illis bonis rebus multo esse meliorem: ita in hac mundi domo, cum coelum terramque perspicias, providentiam, ordinem, legem, crede esse universitatis dominum parentemque ipsis sideribus et totius mundi partibus pulchriorem. Ni forte, quoniam de providentia nulla dubitatio est, inquirendum putas, utrum unius imperio, an arbitrio plurimorum coeleste regnum gubernetur: quod ipsum non est multi laboris aperire cogitanti imperia terrena, quibus exempla utique de coelo: quando umquam regni societas aut cum fide coepit, aut sine cruore discessit? Omitto Persas, de equorum hinnitu augurantes principatum; et Thebanorum permortuam fabulam, transeo: ob pastorum et casae regnum de geminis memoria notissima est; generi et soceri bella toto orbe diffusa sunt: et tam magni imperii duos fortuna non cepit. Vide caetera: rex unus apibus, dux unus gregibus, in armentis rector unus: tu in coelo summam potestatem dividi credas, et scindi veri illius ac divini imperii totam potestatem? cum palam sit parentem omnium Deum nec principium habere, nec terminum; qui nativitatem24 omnibus praestet, sibi perpetuitatem, qui ante mundum fuerit sibi ipse pro mundo; qui universa, quaecumque sunt, verbo jubet, ratione dispensat, virtute consummat. Hic nec videri potest, visu clarior est; nec comprehendi, tactu purior est; nec aestimari, sensibus major est, infinitus, immensus, et soli sibi, tantus quantus est, notus; nobis vero ad intellectum pectus angustum est; et ideo sic eum digne aestimamus dum inaestimabilem dicimus. Eloquar quemadmodum sentio; magnitudinem Dei qui se putat nosse, minuit; qui non vult minuere, non novit. Nec nomen Deo quaeras, Deus nomen est. Illic vocabulis opus est cum per singulos propriis appellationum insignibus multitudo dirimenda est: Deo, qui solus est, Dei vocabulum totum est. Quem si patrem dixero, terrenum opineris; si regem, carnalem suspiceris; si dominum, intelliges utique mortalem. Aufer additamenta nominum, et perspicies ejus claritatem. Quid? quod omnium de isto habeo consensum: audio vulgus, quum ad coelum manus tendunt, nihil aliud quam DEUM dicunt; et, DEUS MAGNUS EST; et, DEUS VERUS EST, et, SI DEUS DEDERIT. Vulgi iste naturalis sermo est, an Christiani confitentis oratio? et qui Jovem principem volunt, falluntur in nomine, sed de una potestate consentiunt.
pass_a_gloss: It is long to go through individual things: there is nothing in man of members, which is not both for the cause of necessity and of decoration: and what is more wonderful, the same figure for all, but certain lineaments are bent for each one. Thus we seem similar to all, and among themselves we are found dissimilar in individual things. What is the reason of being born? What is the desire of generating? Is it not given by God? And so that breasts with parturition maturing become milky, and so that the tender foal with the abundance of milky dew grows up? Nor does God consult for the universe alone, but also for the parts. Britain is deficient in sun, but is restored by the warmth of the surrounding sea: the Nile river tempers the dryness of Egypt: the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia: the Indus compensates for the rains, and is said to sow and to water the East. But if you had entered some house, and had seen all things cultivated, arranged, adorned, you would certainly believe that a master is in charge of it, and that he is much better than those good things: so in this house of the world, when you look at the heaven and the earth, believe that there is a master and parent of the universe, and more beautiful than the stars themselves and the parts of the whole world. Unless perhaps, since there is no doubt about providence, you think that it should be investigated, whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one, or by the decision of many: which itself is not much labor to reveal to the thinking person, by means of earthly empires, of which the examples are certainly from heaven: when did the society of a kingdom ever begin with faith, or end without bloodshed? I pass over the Persians, who take the neighing of horses as an omen of rule; and the utterly dead fable of the Thebans, I skip: the memory of the kingdom of the shepherds and the hut is most well-known on account of the twins: wars between son-in-law and father-in-law have been spread throughout the whole world: and fortune has not captured two such great empires. See the rest: one king for the bees, one leader for the flocks, one ruler for the herds: do you believe that the highest power is divided in heaven, and that the whole power of that true and divine empire is torn apart? When it is clear that God is the parent of all, and has neither beginning nor end; who provides birth for all, perpetuity for himself, who was before the world for himself as the world; who commands all things, whatever they are, by his word, dispenses by his reason, completes by his power. This one cannot be seen, is clearer than sight; cannot be comprehended, is purer than touch; cannot be estimated, is greater than the senses, infinite, immeasurable, and known only to himself, so great as he is; for us, indeed, the breast is narrow for understanding; and therefore we esteem him worthily when we say that he is inestimable. I will speak as I think; whoever thinks that he knows the magnitude of God, diminishes it; whoever does not want to diminish it, does not know it. Nor should you seek a name for God, God is a name. There, words are necessary when a multitude must be distinguished by individual marks of appellations: for God, who is alone, the whole word is God. If I call him Father, you will think of an earthly one; if King, you will suspect a carnal one; if Lord, you will understand a mortal one. Remove the additions of names, and you will see his clarity. What? Since I have consensus from all about this: I hear the common people, when they stretch out their hands to heaven, say nothing other than GOD; and, GOD IS GREAT; and, GOD IS TRUE; and, IF GOD GIVES. Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the confession of a Christian? And those who want Jupiter to be the ruler, are deceived in the name, but consent to one power.

pass_b_english: Going through each part one by one would take too long: there is not a single member in the human body that does not serve both necessity and beauty. What is more astonishing, we all share the same basic form, yet each person's features are distinctly shaped. Thus we appear alike as a species, but we are found different from one another in every detail. What is the reason for being born? What is the drive to procreate? Is it not given by God? And so that breasts become milky as childbirth matures, and so that the tender offspring grows strong on the abundance of milky dew? God provides not only for the whole, but also for the parts. Britain lacks sun, yet is restored by the warmth of the surrounding sea; the Nile tempers Egypt's dryness; the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia; the Indus makes up for the rains, and is said to sow and water the East. If you entered a house and saw everything cultivated, arranged, and adorned, you would certainly believe a master is in charge of it, and that he is far better than those good things themselves. So it is in this house of the world: when you look at heaven and earth, believe there is a master and parent of the universe, more beautiful than the stars themselves and all the parts of the whole world. Unless perhaps, since there is no doubt about providence, you think we should investigate whether the heavenly kingdom is governed by the command of one or by the decision of many. That question itself is not hard to resolve for a thinking person, using earthly empires as examples—examples that certainly come from heaven. When did a partnership in ruling ever begin in good faith, or end without bloodshed? I pass over the Persians, who read the rule in the neighing of horses; and the utterly dead fable of the Thebans, I skip. The memory of the kingdom born of the shepherds and the hut is most famous because of the twins; wars between son-in-law and father-in-law have spread throughout the whole world, and fortune has not managed to seize two such great empires. Look at the rest: one king for the bees, one leader for the flocks, one ruler for the herds—yet you believe the highest power is divided in heaven, and that the whole power of that true and divine empire is torn apart? When it is clear that God is the parent of all and has neither beginning nor end; who gives birth to all, perpetuity to himself, who existed before the world for himself as the world; who commands all things by his word, dispenses them by his reason, completes them by his power. He cannot be seen, yet is clearer than sight; cannot be grasped, yet is purer than touch; cannot be measured, yet is greater than the senses, infinite, immeasurable, and known only to himself, as great as he is. For us, indeed, the heart is too narrow for understanding; therefore we esteem him worthily only when we call him inestimable. I will speak as I think: whoever thinks he knows the magnitude of God diminishes it; whoever refuses to diminish it does not know it. Nor should you seek a name for God—God is the name. Words are necessary where a multitude must be distinguished by individual marks of names: for God, who is alone, the whole word is God. If I call him Father, you will think of an earthly one; if King, you will suspect a carnal one; if Lord, you will understand a mortal one. Remove the additions of names, and you will see his clarity. What? Since I have the consensus of all on this: I hear the common people, when they stretch out their hands to heaven, say nothing other than GOD; and GOD IS GREAT; and GOD IS TRUE; and IF GOD GIVES. Is this the natural speech of the common people, or the confession of a Christian? And those who want Jupiter to be the ruler are deceived in the name, but they consent to one power.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the sequence of 'providentiam, ordinem, legem' (providence, order, law) which Pass B slightly streamlines, but Pass B remains faithful to the sense. The translation of 'pectus' as 'breast' in Pass A and 'heart' in Pass B is a valid stylistic variation for the anatomical/metaphorical sense of the chest/heart area. All theological nuances regarding God's nature and the arguments regarding earthly vs. heavenly rule are preserved.
